title: Gideon and the Verdict
premise: Estate lawyer Odile Vasquez is summoned to probate the will of Marisol Reyes, a woman declared legally dead seven years ago—yet the will is dated three years after her disappearance. Digging through Marisol's effects, Odile finds a diary whose entries continue past the disappearance date, written in a hand that grows shakier, then stops mid-sentence. As Odile follows the diary's trail through a corrupt land-development scheme Marisol was quietly documenting, they realize the killer has been one step ahead all along: someone with access to the original case file is erasing witnesses and forging documents faster than Odile can find them. The trap Odile sets—using the contested will as bait—draws the killer into the open at the reading of the estate, where justice arrives not by verdict but by confession recorded, and Odile must choose between handing evidence to the police who failed Marisol or letting an accomplice-victim walk free.
about_author: Ada Vane spent a decade as a paralegal in probate court before turning to fiction, and her novels are known for their forensic attention to paperwork as crime scene. She lives in a coastal town she refuses to name, citing 'ongoing matters.'

chapters.title: The Will That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Odile Vasquez, POV. A courier delivers a will for Marisol Reyes—declared dead seven years ago—with a signature date three years after her disappearance. Odile's firm wants it refused; something in the document's formatting nags at them. Emotional beat: professional unease curdling into obsession.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Missing Woman
chapters.summary: Odile visits the sealed storage unit holding Marisol's effects and finds the diary among boxed linens. The final visible entry is dated four years after the disappearance. Flashbacks establish Odile's own history of staying invisible in a hostile profession. Beat: dread mixed with recognition.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Odile reads the diary through the night. Early entries describe a happy bookkeeper; later ones describe being watched, payments from Halcyon Development, a man called 'the Auditor.' The handwriting deteriorates. Beat: the thrill of discovery shadowed by fear of what watching means.

chapters.title: The Detective Who Closed the File
chapters.summary: Odile tracks down Ray Okonkwo, the retired detective who closed Marisol's case as a voluntary disappearance. He is defensive, drunk, and lets slip that the case file was requested—and returned—by someone official two years ago. Beat: bitter alliance forming between two people who failed her.

chapters.title: Halcyon Rising
chapters.summary: Odile researches Halcyon Development, which razed Marisol's neighborhood for a marina project. Two other residents who filed complaints died in 'accidents.' The diary's numbers match missing escrow funds. Beat: the scale of corruption becomes clear; power, not passion, killed Marisol.

chapters.title: A Visitor Signs the Guest Book
chapters.summary: Someone breaks into Odile's office but takes nothing—only photographs the will and leaves the guest book signed with Marisol's name. Odile realizes the killer knows exactly what they have. First-person plural shifts to close third as Odile stops sleeping. Beat: hunted.

chapters.title: The Auditor's Ledger
chapters.summary: Following a diary clue to a defunct credit union, Odile retrieves a microfiche ledger listing payoffs—including one to a county clerk who forged the death certificate. The clerk, alive and terrified, confirms someone recently bought her silence again. Beat: hope that the conspiracy is still active, and therefore stoppable.

chapters.title: What Ray Buried
chapters.summary: Ray confesses he was pressured to close the case by his captain, now a Halcyon consultant. He kept a copy of the original file as insurance. Before he can hand it over, his apartment is ransacked; the copy is gone. Beat: guilt and rage; the enemy is always ahead.

chapters.title: Diary of the Living
chapters.summary: A new entry appears in Marisol's diary—fresh ink, planted in Odile's car. It warns: 'Stop, or you'll be a footnote too.' Forensics confirm the handwriting is learned imitation. The killer is taunting, which means the diary matters to them. Beat: terror weaponized into resolve.

chapters.title: The Second Will
chapters.summary: Odile discovers the delivered will itself is a forgery—but a forgery built on a real document. Someone wanted the estate opened, forcing the diary into legal record where it could be seized and destroyed. The trap runs both directions. Beat: intellectual reversal; the case file knows them better than they know it.

chapters.title: Witnesses in Order of Death
chapters.summary: Mapping the diary against obituaries, Odile realizes the victims were killed in the order they appear as witnesses in the forged will. The next name is a living woman: Elena Cruz, Marisol's former coworker. Beat: racing-clock urgency begins.

chapters.title: Elena
chapters.summary: Odile finds Elena Cruz hiding in a motel, paying cash, feeding a stray cat. Elena saw the Auditor's face seven years ago and has been running since. She reveals Marisol didn't disappear—she went underground with copies of everything, and contacted Elena weeks ago. Beat: fragile trust; the price of survival made flesh.

chapters.title: Where Marisol Went
chapters.summary: Elena leads Odile to Marisol's last known refuge: a houseboat sold under a false name. Inside, signs of hurried departure and a hidden compartment—empty except for a single key tagged with a probate case number. Beat: grief; Marisol was here, recently, and ran again.

chapters.title: The Case Number
chapters.summary: The key opens a safe-deposit box at the same credit union—registered under the forged will's case number, meaning the killer opened it after Marisol vanished from it. Inside: nothing but a mirror. The killer anticipated this exact search. Beat: humiliation and chilling admiration for the adversary.

chapters.title: Reading the Enemy
chapters.summary: Odile profiles the killer from the forgeries' habits: legal training, access to the closed case file, knowledge of probate procedure. The list narrows to three people connected to both Halcyon and the courthouse—including Odile's own managing partner. Beat: paranoia; nowhere is neutral ground.

chapters.title: The Partner
chapters.summary: Confronting the partner goes wrong—he has an alibi and, worse, he reveals Odile was assigned the Reyes will deliberately. Someone inside chose them. Odile realizes they aren't the investigator; they're the fall guy. Beat: betrayal, isolation, the floor dropping out.

chapters.title: Bait
chapters.summary: Odile flips the dynamic: publicly announces a formal reading of the Reyes estate, knowing the killer must attend to control the record. With Ray and Elena, they stage the event, seed it with a fake diary page, and arrange quiet recording. Beat: cold courage; hunters becoming bait.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: The estate reading proceeds like a séance. Attendees include the captain, a Halcyon lawyer, and Judge Aldous Wren—the presiding judge who certified Marisol's death. When the fake page surfaces, Wren's procedural objections betray knowledge no innocent reader could have. Beat: taut, theatrical tension.

chapters.title: The Auditor Unmasked
chapters.summary: Wren, cornered by the recording and Ray's testimony, unravels: he was the Auditor, laundering Halcyon's payoffs through the court, and he murdered Marisol when she tried to come back for her money—her 'death' was his masterpiece. He lunges for the diary; Elena stops him. Beat: violent climax; justice seizing its moment outside protocol.

chapters.title: What the Recording Owes
chapters.summary: With Wren arrested, the dilemma lands: the recording also implicates Elena in years of document fraud committed to survive. Handing everything to prosecutors destroys her; withholding makes Odile what they hunted. Odile edits nothing but gives the diary itself to Marisol's only heir. Beat: moral weight of every choice.

chapters.title: Verdict Outside the Courtroom
chapters.summary: Wren pleads to lesser charges when the diary surfaces publicly via the heir, gutting Halcyon's marina project and reopening the deaths of the neighborhood complainants. Elena, quietly, leaves town with a new name Odile helped forge—their first dishonest act, freely chosen. Beat: bittersweet resolution; the law served, imperfectly.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Odile closes the estate and reads the diary's true final page, tucked in the binding: Marisol knew she might not survive coming back, and wrote it anyway so someone would finish the sentence. Odile adds their own line beneath it and files the will as genuine. Beat: quiet catharsis; visibility chosen over safety.
